(Today through Monday)...
Issued at 139 AM EDT Tue Aug 11 2026

Overview.

Severe weather is likely today with a complex of storms moving in 
from the northwest. Repeated rounds of thunderstorms are expected to 
continue through Wednesday night with lower chances through the 
remainder of the week. Damaging winds and flooding will be the main 
threats today and tomorrow. Outside of storms, heat will be a 
concern today with heat index values up to 105 in southwest Indiana.

Today Through Tonight.

Central Indiana remains positioned along the northeastern periphery 
of a strong subtropical ridge centered over the southern Plains, 
maintaining an active northwest flow regime aloft. Low-level WAA and 
moisture transport continue to stream across the region, yielding 
surface dewpoints in the mid-70s and PWAT values approaching 2.0 to 
2.2 inches. Strong diurnal heating will destabilize the boundary 
layer today, yielding SBCAPE values exceeding 3500-4500 J/kg by 
afternoon. High temperatures rising into the upper 80s to low 90s 
combined with elevated humidity will create heat index values near 
105 degrees, particularly across southern and central counties. A 
Heat Advisory is in effect for southwestern Indiana from 12PM to 
9PM. 

Convective initiation and timing remain tied to subtle shortwaves 
riding the ridge edge and residual boundaries from previous
storms.

00Z model guidance actually is in fairly good agreement on the 
broader timing for convection through daybreak and into today, but 
differ on the exact details. Broadly, there is good agreement in 
initiation continuing over the next couple of hours over northern 
Illinois/northern Indiana, likely along the remnant outflow boundary 
from the earlier convection. Some models have this quickly growing 
upscale into an MCS that dives south, but with the fairly stable 
near surface, expect these storms to remain elevated and generally 
sub-severe. The second round would then initiate across eastern Iowa 
and northern Illinois towards mid-morning with quick upscale growth 
into an MCS and an arrival near the I-74 corridor towards the late 
afternoon to early evening. By the time storms arrive SB CAPE values 
will be in excess of 3500 J/kg across central Indiana with 
sufficient shear to maintain an organized MCS with the potential for 
widespread damaging winds. If storms through daybreak do end up 
growing upscale, this could delay the second round by a few hours, 
but with the very humid airmass, it looks unlikely that any morning 
convection would significantly lower any risk later in the day.

Regardless of timing, heavy rainfall and flash flooding will be 
another significant concern. High freezing levels above 14,000 
feet and deep warm-rain processes combined with the potential for 
training convective cores along the western periphery of the 
complex raise flash flood potential. HREF probability matched mean
guidance indicates localized rainfall totals of 2 to 4 inches 
where storm training occurs. With that in mind, a Flood Watch is 
in effect from 12PM through 10PM with the potential need for an 
extension or additional watch for Wednesday.

Wednesday Through Monday.

The active synoptic configuration persists into Wednesday as central 
Indiana stays situated in the baroclinic gradient on the eastern 
flank of the southern ridge. Global guidance, including the GFS and 
ECMWF, depicts a prominent mid-level trough digging from the Upper 
Midwest into the Great Lakes on Wednesday. This wave will help to 
push the aforementioned surface cold front southward through the CWA 
late Wednesday through early Thursday morning. Deep-layer moisture 
remains unseasonably high across the southern half of the forecast 
area with PWATs lingering near 2.0 inches ahead of the boundary. The 
combination of frontal forcing, upper-level jet divergence, and 
moderate instability will generate another round of showers and 
thunderstorms Wednesday afternoon and night. The GEFS and EPS 
ensemble means show strong agreement on severe weather and heavy 
rainfall potential continuing along and south of I-70 until frontal 
passage occurs early Thursday.

By Thursday night into Friday, model guidance agrees on the southward 
progression of the surface cold front into the Ohio Valley, bringing 
at least some minor relief from the hot and humid conditions. High 
temperatures Thursday and Friday will moderate into the low to mid-
80s with dewpoints dropping into the upper 60s to low 70s for all 
but the southern portions of the state. Low-end chance PoPs are 
maintained across southern counties beginning Friday morning to 
account for residual elevated moisture and minor shortwave energy 
overriding the frontal zone, but the overall threat for severe 
weather and flash flooding will wane significantly.
